job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a regional engineering firm in Dayton, Ohio, doing road and drainage design for the county. I do takeoffs, which means counting how much asphalt, pipe and gravel a project needs, and I draw the plans in CAD. Twice a week I'm out in a hard hat checking that the contractor poured what we drew. I share a rental house with two guys from church, and on Sundays I'm at services and then dinner at my fiancée Hannah's parents' place. We want to marry next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype was too much. At work I'd keep doing what we do, because counties don't buy a new way of working every year. At church I'd say nothing changes about what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel steady. Roads still get built, and the county still needs somebody to check them. My worry is money for the wedding and a house, since interest rates make a mortgage in Dayton hard even with my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and saving. I'd put away money each month for a down payment, and I'd study for the PE licence, the professional engineer exam, which I can take in four years. I wouldn't change how I use computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A man should be able to count on his work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mortgage. How does that look for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah's a teacher's aide, so we'd have two modest incomes. A starter house is about 220,000 and we'd need around 45,000 down. We've got 28,000 between us, with her dad offering to help, but I'd rather earn it than ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the PE licence do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me stamp drawings, and it bumps pay by about a fifth. Plus it's a thing nobody can take away. My uncle is a PE, and he says the licence is the closest thing in this trade to owning land.

say: The hype was too much, and nothing changes about **what matters**.
Counties don't buy a new way of working every year.
think: Roads still need somebody to **check them**, so I feel steady.
My real worry is a **mortgage** with today's interest rates.
do: Save each month toward a **down payment** of about 45,000.
Study for the **PE licence** and take the exam in four years.
feel: I feel **calm**, because a man should count on his work.
S0.quote: My uncle is a PE, and he says the licence is the closest thing in this trade to owning land.
fieldNote: He is secure because county work is **slow-moving** and licensed.
His pressure is the wedding and the first house.
He would prefer to earn rather than ask his future father-in-law.

steps.text: Save 1,000 a month toward a 45,000 house down payment
Study for the PE licence exam in the evenings
Keep doing takeoffs and site checks for the county

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software is going to take some jobs, but not the ones where you need boots on the ground. At work I'd say we should be careful about trusting it with drainage calculations, because that's how a basement floods. At church I'd say work still matters and pride in work still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the takeoffs and the drawings are the parts a program can do, so a firm could need fewer people at desks. My boss Gary says he'd never let a program stamp a plan, and I believe him, but he's also 61 and he'd retire before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick with my routine and spend more time on site, because that's what the program can't do. I'd also take the courses the firm offers, even though I don't love them. And I'd move the wedding plans along, because I don't want to wait on the world to settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'm not afraid, but I don't love how fast people talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't love the firm's courses. What puts you off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like learning from a person in a room and learning from a manual. Videos with a voice telling me to click the next thing feel hollow. But I know I'd have to, and I'd rather be the one who knows than the one who's told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gary would retire before it hits. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me think the older ones will say it's fine and the younger ones will take the heat. I'd tell Gary straight that I need him to teach me his judgement before he goes. A site walk with my boss is worth a year of videos.

say: Software will take some jobs, but not where you need **boots on the ground**.
I'd be careful trusting it with drainage, because that's how a basement floods.
think: Takeoffs and drawings are what a program can do, so fewer people at **desks**.
Gary will retire before it hits, and the **younger ones** take the heat.
do: Spend more time on **site**, where a program can't go.
Take the firm's **courses** and ask Gary to teach me his judgement.
S1.quote: A site walk with my boss is worth a year of videos.
fieldNote: He leans on **site work and mentors**, the traditional way to learn.
He senses a gap between older and younger staff.
His unease is mild because of licensing and hands-on work.

steps.text: Ask my boss Gary for monthly site walks to learn his judgement
Take the firm's software courses even though I dislike them
Do more site inspections than desk takeoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to take in two years and it needs a steady hand. At church I'd say pray and be ready to help neighbours. At work I'd say we shouldn't rush to let a computer do the stamping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. Thinking work is done by a machine within two years, so my desk is gone, and the county might not hire for a long time. Hands-on work lasts longer, but I'm a designer, not a pipe layer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the wedding date for a bit, or have a small one. I'd stick to my savings and maybe take a second job on weekends, working for a contractor on site. I'd also talk to Hannah and her dad about whether it's better to rent for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty heavy. I don't like feeling that my plans depend on something I can't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off the wedding date. What would you say to Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I love her and I don't want to start our life afraid. We'd do something small and keep savings for the thing we can't predict. She'd say we have each other, which she says whenever I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would working on site on weekends look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the contractor I know, Mike, if he needs a foreman's helper or someone to check quantities. It pays little, but I'd learn how a crew works. If the desk goes, I'd have a step into construction management.

say: It's a lot to take in two years and needs a **steady hand**.
I'd say pray, help neighbours and don't rush to let a computer stamp plans.
think: Thinking work is done by a machine within two years, so my **desk** could be gone.
Hands-on work lasts longer, but I'm a **designer**, not a pipe layer.
do: Keep the wedding **small** and hold savings for what I can't predict.
Take weekend work on **site** with a contractor.
feel: I feel **heavy**, because my plans depend on things I can't control.
S2.quote: I don't want to start our life afraid.
fieldNote: He still holds to **marriage** but shrinks the plan.
His fall-back is moving to construction, a physical field.
Faith and his **fiancée** give him steadiness, and he plans to keep the wedding but make it smaller.

steps.text: Keep the wedding small and book the church hall instead of a venue
Ask Mike for weekend work on site
Rent for two more years before buying a house
Put every spare dollar into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent amount of time, and people should use it. At work I'd say we should invest in training instead of firing. At church I'd tell people to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious about year three or four, but I'd see a path. I'd want to move from desk design to construction management, which is hands-on and people-heavy. That's the stuff that lasts longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study for the PE exam sooner, then take a construction management certificate. I'd get married as planned and buy a modest house in three years. I'd learn what I need on the computer, but I'd lean on people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little anxious, but not afraid. Five years is enough to do right by Hannah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why construction management in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's where a good name matters. A foreman knows who's honest, who shows up and who's cutting corners. A program doesn't know a guy from a hole in the ground. That's a trade I could do for forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the computer skills you said you'd learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course on the design software the firm uses and nothing fancy. I'm not interested in chatting with a bot, but I'd learn what's needed to do the job. I think a man can respect new tools without trusting everything about them.

say: Five years is decent, and the firm should **train** instead of firing.
I'd tell people at church to look after each other.
think: I'd be anxious about year three or four, but I see a path into **construction management**.
Hands-on work with people lasts longest.
do: Sit the **PE exam** sooner, then a construction management certificate.
Marry as planned and buy a modest **house** in three years.
feel: I feel **a little anxious**, not afraid.
S3.quote: A program doesn't know a guy from a hole in the ground.
fieldNote: He plans a **trade move** toward hands-on supervision.
He trusts reputation, not software, to judge people.
He accepts only the computer skills the job requires.

steps.text: Take the PE exam within two years
Buy a modest house in three years
Learn the firm's design software and nothing more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and I wouldn't change plans much. At work I'd say train people. At church I'd say keep working and don't be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly okay. By 32 I'd have the PE, maybe a couple of kids, and a house. The future might not look like today, but a man with skills and a good name finds work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my plans, add construction management and maybe run a small firm someday. I'd save for the kids' college. I'd learn the new tools gradually and let others test them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. I think it'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe running a small firm someday. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four or five guys, doing county and small-town work, all of us knowing the people we work for, drainage and roads. I'd want to pay a fair wage and take apprentices. My grandfather had a hardware store like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you say to friends who are afraid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait around to be rescued, learn something solid and keep your word. Government can't fix everything, but neighbours can help each other. I'd offer to mentor a younger guy from church.

say: Ten years is a **lot of time**, so I wouldn't change plans much.
I'd tell people at church to keep working and not be afraid.
think: By 32 I'd hold the **PE**, maybe have kids and own a house.
A man with skills and a **good name** finds work.
do: Add construction management and maybe run a **small firm** someday with a few good men.
Save for the kids' **college** from the first year.
feel: I feel **steady**, as if it would be fine.
S4.quote: Four or five guys, doing county and small-town work, all of us knowing the people we work for, drainage and roads.
fieldNote: Ten years confirms his **small-firm ideal** of local work.
His answer to fear is skills, reputation and neighbours.
He still lets others test new tools first.

steps.text: Finish the PE and construction management certificate in the next five years
Mentor one younger man from church in the trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Two years is too fast for a young couple trying to buy a house. What would help is steady interest rates, training that comes with a job and employers who keep faith with their people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people think a man like me doesn't care about tech. I care. I just want to see it work before I trust it with other people's drainage.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the one who knows than the one who's told.
portrait: Sam is a **22-year-old** civil engineer at a county design firm in Dayton, engaged to Hannah.
He is traditional, church-going, favours work and apprenticeships, and **never uses AI**.
His anchor is the **PE licence**, site work and a mentor, not tools.
He is calm with little change, and **anxious** when two years threaten his house and wedding plans.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because it threatens his wedding and house plans.
whatWouldHelp: **Steady interest rates**, training tied to a job and employers who keep faith.
